b: Ryan Park knew he was rolling the dice when he left Charlotte in search of a lake he had never fished before. He met up half way with one of his old college fishing partners that left from Tennessee. The trip came together after the two had spent weeks digging through online articles and social media posts about a little-known public lake in southeast Florida. The nameless lake had the reputation of producing giant largemouth bass. Between the gas, the time off work and the long drive down, the friends were, as Park put it, “betting the house on this lake producing.”

Park, 25, is no stranger to catching big bass. He won a high school state championship as a sophomore and fished all four years for Murray State University’s team. He now coaches a high school bass fishing team. Still, his personal best largemouth stood at 7.67 pounds heading into the trip, and he was hoping Florida would change that.
Park holds up one of several 8-pounders he caught during the trip.

Park set up camp at an Airbnb near the lake, a move he swears by for any serious bass trip. “Airbnb is the best thing that ever happened to bass fishing,” he said. “I’m a lot more confident my boat and equipment are going to be there in the morning.”

The first afternoon was mostly about learning the water. By the time they launched, the day was already getting late, and Park was still getting used to the LiveScope setup on a friend’s boat. The bites that did come were small.

“All I was catching were one- and two-pounders,” Park said. “I remember thinking, ‘OK, we’ve got to get something figured out here.’” Still, there were a few signs of life on the screen. “We saw some dots out there moving around,” he said. “They probably weren’t in the right areas, but it gave us enough hope.”
The borrowed pink urchin bait sits deep in the mouth of a big largemouth, showing these bass weren’t messing around.

The second morning started slow, too, until Park eased up on an underwater point and spotted two big dots hovering far out on his LiveScope. He reached for a Coike. Parks said he likes to work the Coike like a jerkbait. But unlike a jerkbait, the urchin bait suspends in one place which lets him keep it hovering above a fish’s head until the fish commits. “I’ve noticed If it’s above their heads, they’ll come up to get it,” Park said. “They just don’t like it when it sinks down to the bottom.”

Park made a long cast, and as soon as the lure hit the surface, both dots disappeared from the screen as they made a beeline for the bait. A couple of twitches later, a big bass came up and inhaled it. “It came out of the water way out there, and I knew right then it was a new personal best,” Park said.

After a long fight, he landed a toad that weighed about 9½ pounds, his new personal best and the reason he drove all the way to Florida. Around the same time, his buddy called to say he had just caught a 7-pounder. “That’s when we knew we had them figured out,” Park said. “That’s exactly what we came down there for.” The group kept catching good fish into the afternoon, until a storm rolled in and chased everyone off the water.
Park eases up on an underwater point where he spots two big dots hovering far out.

Before the storm hit, Park had spotted three huge dots sitting on a brush pile, the biggest he had ever seen on LiveScope. When the weather cleared that evening, the group headed straight back to find out what they were. Park eased up to the brush pile and reached for a pink Coike. It wasn’t even his. He couldn’t find one online before the trip, so he borrowed it from one of the high school anglers he coaches.
He launched the bait more than 100 feet and started working it with a steady cadence. At first, the fish didn’t budge. Then all three slowly started rolling toward it, and two of them picked up speed.

“They were completely locked in on that pink Coike,” Park said. “I just tried to stay calm and keep working at it, because when you watch them get that close on LiveScope, it’s easy to get excited and mess it up.”

When the fish were about 30 feet from the boat, Park went to pop the bait and felt nothing. He popped it again, and it was just heavy. He set the hook, and the bass shot out of the water so close to the boat that it nearly hit the trolling motor.

The fish dove under the boat and came up on the other side, where Park and his buddy could hear it shaking its head on the surface. After a strong fight, Park finally worked the bass to the top, and his friend scooped it up in one swoop of the net.

The largemouth weighed 12 pounds and dwarfed the 9½-pounder from that morning. Park said it looked like it had already spawned, and with its huge frame, it likely would have been closer to 14 pounds before it did. “We just started laughing hysterically, because we couldn’t believe what we were looking at,” Park said. “I told my buddy, ‘This doesn’t even look like a bass.’”
By the end of the trip, Park added an 11-pounder to his catches, and the gamble on a lake none of them had ever seen had paid off in a big way.
